patient_counselling: Take a non-sedating second-generation antihistamine DAILY (regularly, not just when itchy): cetirizine 10 mg OD, loratadine 10 mg OD, fexofenadine 120–180 mg OD, bilastine 20 mg OD, or rupatadine 10 mg OD. Daily prophylactic dosing is more effective than PRN.

If standard dose isn't controlling symptoms after 2–4 weeks, the antihistamine can be UP-DOSED up to 4× the standard dose (off-label but evidence-based per EAACI 2022 / CSACI) — confirm with pharmacist or physician before doing this.

Avoid first-generation antihistamines (diphenhydramine/Benadryl, hydroxyzine) for routine use — sedation, anticholinergic effects (dry mouth, urinary retention), and Beers Criteria caution in older adults; reserve for short-term sleep aid only.

Identify and avoid triggers if known: foods (shellfish, nuts, eggs, food additives), medications (NSAIDs, ASA, opioids, ACE inhibitors), infections (viral most common), physical triggers (cold, heat, pressure, sunlight, exercise), stress.
Cool compresses, loose cotton clothing, and lukewarm (not hot) showers help reduce itching. Avoid harsh soaps and skin irritants. Add colloidal oatmeal to bathwater for comfort.

Most acute urticaria resolves within 6 weeks. If hives persist longer than 6 weeks (chronic urticaria), referral to allergist/dermatologist is needed — may benefit from omalizumab (Xolair) third-line therapy.

Common antihistamine side effects: cetirizine — mild drowsiness in some (take at bedtime); loratadine/fexofenadine/bilastine — minimal sedation. Take fexofenadine on empty stomach (avoid with fruit juice). Bilastine: take 1 hour before or 2 hours after food.

Red flags — call 911 immediately: difficulty breathing or swallowing, throat tightness, swelling of lips/tongue/face (angioedema with airway risk), wheezing, dizziness/fainting, rapid pulse — these are signs of anaphylaxis, not simple urticaria.

Return to pharmacy if: hives persist >6 weeks despite up-dosed antihistamines, hives leave bruising/staining (suggests urticarial vasculitis — refer), individual lesions last >24 hours in one location.
Store antihistamines at room temperature; keep out of children's reach (especially cetirizine which is sometimes flavoured).
therapeutic_flow: 1. Confirm Minor Ailments eligibility: Ontario resident with typical urticarial presentation (transient, itchy, raised wheals); verify ID/OHIP, obtain consent.

2. Focused history: onset and duration (acute <6 weeks vs chronic ≥6 weeks), individual lesion duration (<24h favours urticaria; >24h or bruising suggests urticarial vasculitis), trigger identification, associated angioedema, prior episodes, atopy history, current medications, pregnancy/lactation.

3. Red flag screen: airway involvement (lip/tongue/throat swelling, dyspnea, stridor, wheezing — call 911), anaphylaxis features (cardiovascular collapse, GI symptoms), individual lesions >24h or with bruising/pigmentation (urticarial vasculitis — refer), suspected drug-induced angioedema (ACEi) — refer.
4. Differential diagnosis: rule out urticarial vasculitis, mastocytosis, contact dermatitis, drug eruption, viral exanthem, autoimmune urticaria, physical urticaria subtypes, hereditary angioedema.

5. Therapy selection: 2nd-generation H1-antihistamine at standard dose × 2–4 weeks; if inadequate, up-dose to 2–4× standard dose per EAACI 2022; identify/eliminate triggers; avoid NSAIDs/ASA which can worsen urticaria.
6. Counsel on daily dosing (not PRN), trigger avoidance, supportive measures (cool compresses, loose clothing), expected timeline, anaphylaxis warning signs, when to return.
7. Document the encounter per OCP standards: assessment findings (acute vs chronic, angioedema present or absent), diagnosis, therapy chosen, counselling provided, notify primary care provider.
8. Follow-up: reassess at 2–4 weeks; if persistent ≥6 weeks (chronic urticaria) or refractory to up-dosed antihistamines, refer to allergist or dermatologist for omalizumab consideration.
